name: Jefferson curl

card.summary: A loaded spinal-flexion mobility exercise popular in strength circles; barely studied, with one small 2026 EMG study to date.
card.aka: Loaded spinal flexion, weighted forward fold
card.note: Deliberately loads the spine in flexion, a position many clinicians and lifters treat cautiously; published research is minimal.

quick.overview:
The Jefferson curl is a strength and mobility exercise in which a person slowly rolls the spine into flexion while holding a light weight, then returns to standing. It is discussed in strength-training, rehabilitation and posture communities as a way to build hamstring and back flexibility and posterior-chain tolerance.

Research is very thin. A 2026 study characterised erector spinae muscle activity during the exercise compared with the Romanian deadlift, and described the exercise as popular but lacking empirical characterisation. No trial found tests it for posture or appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say gradual loaded flexion through a controlled range increases flexibility and conditions the spine's tissues. Researchers have so far only measured muscle activation during the movement and compared it with a hip-hinge lift.
quick.risks: Loaded spinal flexion is a movement pattern that some clinicians and coaches advise caution with, particularly for people with back pain. A qualitative study of people with chronic low back pain found participants perceiving some exercises as potentially injurious. No injury-rate data specific to the Jefferson curl were found.

lead: The Jefferson curl is a loaded spinal flexion exercise in which the lifter, standing with a weight, progressively curls the spine forward and down vertebra by vertebra and then reverses the movement. A 2026 paper describes it as having gained popularity in strength and rehabilitation practice but lacking empirical characterisation.[1]

In looksmaxxing and posture circles it is sometimes grouped with mobility work for the posterior chain. The only study identified is a cross-sectional surface electromyography (EMG) study in resistance-trained adults comparing erector spinae activation during the Jefferson curl with a Romanian deadlift at a matched submaximal load.[1] No trial has examined effects on posture or visible appearance.

paras: Unlike a hip hinge, where the spine is held roughly neutral, the Jefferson curl intentionally takes the spine through flexion under load. It is typically performed slowly with a light weight and, according to proponents, aims at hamstring and spinal mobility and tolerance of flexed positions.[1]

A 2026 cross-sectional study in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy used surface EMG in resistance-trained adults to characterise erector spinae activation during the Jefferson curl at a load matched to the Romanian deadlift, testing whether the two exercises differ at the same absolute load.[1] It measured muscle activation only and did not assess long-term mobility, posture, injury or appearance outcomes.

No trials found test the Jefferson curl for posture, flexibility gains or back-pain outcomes. A 2026 exploratory study of breakdancers examined anthropometric and neuromuscular characteristics across performance levels and is only indirectly related to flexibility-oriented training.[2]

No data specific to the Jefferson curl on injury rates were found. A 2025 qualitative study of people with chronic low back pain reported that participants, in the absence of clinical guidance, sometimes perceived certain exercises as risky, with one participant saying they could see themselves getting hurt if they did it wrong.[3] This concerns exercise perception in general rather than this movement specifically.
